# An In-Depth Review of *Middlemarch* by George Eliot

## "The History of Man's Condition": A Comprehensive Critical Examination

---

## Preface: Why *Middlemarch* Demands Our Attention

There is a particular kind of novel that does not merely tell a story but constructs a world so complete, so morally intricate, and so psychologically penetrating that the reader emerges from it changed — not in the dramatic, sudden way of a revelation, but in the slow, accumulative way of genuine experience. George Eliot's *Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life*, published in eight installments between 1871 and 1872, is precisely such a novel. Virginia Woolf called it "one of the few English novels written for grown-up people." Henry James, who was not given to easy praise, described it as "a treasure-house of detail." And yet, despite this critical consensus spanning more than a century and a half, *Middlemarch* remains underread, underappreciated in popular culture, and frequently mischaracterized as a Victorian domestic novel concerned primarily with marriage and social propriety.

This review argues something more ambitious: that *Middlemarch* is the greatest novel in the English language — not because it is the most pleasurable, the most stylistically dazzling, or the most emotionally immediate, but because it achieves something no other English novel has quite managed: a complete, compassionate, and intellectually rigorous account of how human beings actually live, fail, love, compromise, and occasionally transcend themselves within the constraints of society, history, and their own natures. It is a novel about everything that matters, and it treats everything that matters with the seriousness it deserves.

To make this case, I will examine *Middlemarch* across multiple dimensions: its historical and biographical context, its narrative architecture, its major themes, its stylistic innovations, its characterization, its philosophical underpinnings, its reception history, and its enduring relevance. This is not a brief review. *Middlemarch* is not a brief novel. It deserves the time.

---

## Part One: Context — The World That Made the Novel

### George Eliot and the Problem of Being Mary Ann Evans

To understand *Middlemarch*, one must first understand its author, and to understand its author, one must grapple with the extraordinary difficulty of her position. Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880) was born in Warwickshire, England, the daughter of a land agent. She was, by all accounts, an intellectually precocious child who read voraciously and developed, early on, a passionate religious faith that would later be systematically dismantled by her encounter with German biblical criticism and the philosophy of Feuerbach, Spinoza, and Comte.

By her late twenties, Evans had translated Strauss's *Das Leben Jesu* and Feuerbach's *Das Wesen des Christentums* — works that argued, with devastating scholarly rigor, that Christianity was a human construction, that the Gospels were mythological rather than historical, and that the essence of religion was the projection of human ideals onto a divine screen. These translations were not merely academic exercises; they represented Evans's own intellectual and spiritual journey from evangelical Christianity to what she would later call a "religion of humanity" — a secular ethics grounded in sympathy, fellow-feeling, and the recognition of our shared vulnerability.

This philosophical transformation is crucial to understanding *Middlemarch* because the novel is, at its deepest level, a secular scripture — an attempt to do for a post-Christian age what the Bible had done for a Christian one: to provide a moral framework, a set of exemplary lives, and a vision of human dignity that does not depend on supernatural sanction. Eliot's narrator occupies the position of a wise, compassionate, omniscient deity — not the God of judgment and reward, but the God of understanding, who sees all, forgives much, and asks only that we try to see each other clearly.

Evans's personal life was equally unconventional. In 1854, she began a relationship with the philosopher and critic George Henry Lewes, a married man who could not obtain a divorce under Victorian law. Their union, which lasted until Lewes's death in 1878, was a scandal that effectively excluded Evans from polite society. She could not visit friends' homes; she was not received in drawing rooms; she was, in the eyes of Victorian respectability, a fallen woman. The irony — and Eliot was always alert to irony — was that her relationship with Lewes was, by any reasonable moral standard, more genuinely loving, more intellectually equal, and more ethically serious than most of the legal marriages she observed around her.

It was under these circumstances that Mary Ann Evans became "George Eliot" — a male pseudonym adopted partly to ensure her work would be taken seriously, partly to protect Lewes's children from embarrassment, and partly, one suspects, because the freedom of a male identity allowed her to write with an authority and scope that Victorian culture would not easily grant a woman. The pseudonym was eventually an open secret, but it served its purpose: *Scenes of Clerical Life* (1857), *Adam Bede* (1859), *The Mill on the Floss* (1860), *Silas Marner* (1861), *Romola* (1863), *Felix Holt* (1866), and finally *Middlemarch* (1871–72) established "George Eliot" as the preeminent English novelist of the Victorian age.

### The Historical Moment: Reform, Science, and the Crisis of Belief

*Middlemarch* is set in the years 1829–1832, a period of intense political and social ferment in England. The novel's historical backdrop includes the agitation for parliamentary reform that would culminate in the Reform Act of 1832, the early stirrings of the railway age, the ongoing debates about the role of the Church of England, and the beginnings of what would become the Victorian crisis of faith. Eliot chose this period deliberately: it was a moment of transition, when old certainties were dissolving and new possibilities — political, scientific, religious, social — were emerging but not yet consolidated.

The medical subplot involving Tertius Lydgate reflects the actual state of medicine in the early 1830s, when the germ theory of disease had not yet been established, when the distinction between physicians, surgeons, and apothecaries was still legally and socially significant, and when the reform of medical education was a live political issue. Lydgate's ambition to pursue scientific research — specifically, to discover the "primitive tissue" from which all organic life is composed — reflects the actual scientific debates of the period, including the work of Xavier Bichat and the emerging discipline of histology.

The political subplot involving Will Ladislaw and the Reform movement reflects the actual debates of the period, including the arguments about the extension of the franchise, the corruption of "rotten boroughs," and the question of whether political reform could be achieved through constitutional means or required more radical action.

By setting the novel in this specific historical moment, Eliot accomplishes several things simultaneously. She creates a sense of historical depth and specificity that grounds the novel's more abstract concerns in concrete reality. She establishes a parallel between the reform movements of 1829–1832 and the social and intellectual ferment of the 1870s, when the novel was written and published. And she uses the historical distance to achieve a kind of ironic perspective: we know, as the characters do not, how the story of reform will unfold, which allows Eliot to comment on the gap between human aspiration and historical outcome.

---

## Part Two: Architecture — How the Novel Is Built

### The Problem of Structure

*Middlemarch* is a long novel — approximately 900 pages in most modern editions — and its length has sometimes been cited as a barrier to entry. But the length is not padding; it is structural necessity. The novel contains not one plot but four interlocking plots, each of which is complete in itself and each of which illuminates the others through contrast, parallel, and irony.

**Plot One: Dorothea Brooke and Edward Casaubon.** Dorothea, a young woman of passionate idealism and genuine intelligence, marries the elderly scholar Casaubon in the belief that she will be his intellectual partner and that their union will give her life the epic significance she craves. The marriage is a catastrophe — not because Casaubon is a villain, but because he is a disappointed, fearful, emotionally withered man who cannot give Dorothea what she needs and who resents her for needing it.

**Plot Two: Tertius Lydgate and Rosamond Vincy.** Lydgate, a brilliant young doctor with genuine scientific ambitions, marries Rosamond, a beautiful, accomplished, and utterly self-absorbed young woman, in a moment of romantic infatuation. The marriage is also a catastrophe — not because Rosamond is a villain, but because she is a person whose entire moral and emotional world is organized around her own comfort and social position, and who cannot conceive of any claim on her that conflicts with these.

**Plot Three: Fred Vincy and Mary Garth.** Fred, Rosamond's brother, is a charming, feckless young man who loves Mary Garth, a plain, sensible, morally serious young woman who refuses to marry him until he has demonstrated that he can be responsible. This plot is the most conventionally comic of the four, and it provides a kind of moral baseline against which the more tragic plots can be measured.

**Plot Four: Nicholas Bulstrode and John Raffles.** Bulstrode, a wealthy banker and prominent Nonconformist, has built his fortune and his reputation on a foundation of concealed crime. When Raffles, a man who knows his secret, appears in Middlemarch, Bulstrode's carefully constructed identity begins to collapse. This plot is the most melodramatic of the four, and it provides the novel's most direct examination of the relationship between public reputation and private guilt.

### The Weaving of Plots

What makes *Middlemarch* architecturally extraordinary is not the individual plots but the way they are woven together. The four plots are not merely juxtaposed; they are structurally interdependent. Lydgate's financial difficulties, which arise from his marriage to Rosamond, lead him to accept a loan from Bulstrode, which implicates him in Bulstrode's disgrace. Dorothea's inheritance from Casaubon, which is conditional on her not marrying Will Ladislaw, creates the financial pressure that drives the novel's climax. Fred Vincy's debts, which he cannot pay, fall partly on Caleb Garth, whose financial difficulties affect his daughter Mary's relationship with Fred.

These interconnections are not merely plot mechanics; they are thematic statements. The novel argues, through its very structure, that human lives are not isolated units but nodes in a web of mutual dependence and mutual influence. What one person does affects others in ways that are often invisible to the person doing it. The consequences of our choices ripple outward through the social fabric in ways we cannot predict or control. This is not a pessimistic vision — Eliot is not arguing that we are helpless — but it is a vision that insists on the complexity and the weight of moral responsibility.

### The Prelude and the Finale

The novel is framed by a Prelude and a Finale that are among the most important passages in English literature. The Prelude invokes the figure of Saint Theresa of Avila — a woman of "unhistoric acts" who found an "epic life" in the founding of a religious order — and asks what happens to women of similar ardor and vision who are born into a world that offers them no such outlet:

> "Here and there is born a Saint Theresa, foundress of nothing, whose loving heart-beats and sobs after an unattained goodness tremble off and are dispersed among hindrances, instead of centering in some long-recognizable deed."

This passage establishes the novel's central concern: the fate of human aspiration in a world that is indifferent to it, and the question of whether a life can be meaningful even when it fails to achieve the epic significance it sought.

The Finale returns to this question and offers Eliot's answer — an answer that is simultaneously consoling and demanding:

> "Her finely touched spirit had still its fine issues, though they were not widely visible. Her full nature... spent itself in channels which had no great name on the earth. But the effect of her action on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs."

This is one of the most beautiful and most debated passages in Victorian literature. Some readers find it consoling — a validation of the ordinary, a recognition that most human goodness is quiet and unrecorded. Others find it troubling — a rationalization of Dorothea's failure to achieve the epic life she sought, a way of making peace with a world that systematically denies women the opportunity for public achievement. Both readings are legitimate, and the tension between them is part of what makes the passage so powerful.

---

## Part Three: Themes — What the Novel Is About

### Theme One: The Epistemology of Other Minds

If I had to identify the single most important theme in *Middlemarch*, it would be this: the difficulty — and the moral necessity — of truly knowing another person. The novel is obsessed with the gap between how we perceive others and how they actually are, between the stories we tell about people and the reality of their inner lives, between the social masks people wear and the complex, frightened, desiring selves beneath those masks.

This theme is announced early in the novel, in one of Eliot's most famous passages, which describes what it would mean to truly perceive the inner life of another person:

> "If we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life, it would be like hearing the grass grow and the squirrel's heart beat, and we should die of that roar which lies on the other side of silence. As it is, the quickest of us walk about well wadded with stupidity."

This passage is doing several things at once. It is acknowledging the limits of human perception — we cannot fully know another person's inner life, and perhaps it is merciful that we cannot. It is also making a moral argument: our "stupidity" — our failure to perceive the inner lives of others — is not merely an intellectual limitation but a moral one. We fail to see others clearly because it is convenient not to, because truly seeing them would make demands on us that we prefer not to meet.

The novel dramatizes this theme through its treatment of marriage. Both Dorothea's marriage to Casaubon and Lydgate's marriage to Rosamond are failures of perception — failures to see the other person as they actually are rather than as a projection of one's own desires and needs. Dorothea sees Casaubon as a great scholar, a Milton, a man whose intellectual life she can share and serve. She does not see — cannot see, because she has no experience of such things — that he is a man paralyzed by self-doubt, terrified of failure, incapable of genuine intimacy. Lydgate sees Rosamond as a beautiful, accomplished woman who will be a graceful ornament to his life while he pursues his scientific work. He does not see — cannot see, because he has not bothered to look — that she is a person with her own will, her own desires, and her own conception of what her life should be.

The novel's most devastating portrait of failed perception is Casaubon himself. Eliot gives us access to Casaubon's inner life in a way that is almost unbearably compassionate:

> "For my part I am very sorry for him. It is an uneasy lot at best, to be what we call highly taught and yet not to enjoy: to be present at this great spectacle of life and never to be liberated from a small hungry shivering self — never to be fully possessed by the glory we behold, never to have our consciousness rapturously transformed into the vividness of a thought, the ardor of a passion, the energy of an action, but always to be scholarly and uninspired, ambitious and timid, scrupulous and dim-sighted."

This is not the portrait of a villain. It is the portrait of a man who has been failed by his own nature — who wanted to be great and discovered that he was merely competent, who wanted to love and discovered that he could not, who wanted to be admired and discovered that he was pitied. Eliot's compassion for Casaubon is one of the novel's most remarkable achievements, because it asks us to feel for a man who is, in many ways, responsible for Dorothea's suffering. It insists that even the people who hurt us are not simply villains; they are people with their own fears and failures and disappointed hopes.

### Theme Two: Idealism and Its Discontents

*Middlemarch* is a novel about idealism — about what happens to people who want more from life than life is prepared to give them. Dorothea wants an epic life; Lydgate wants to make a great scientific discovery; Will Ladislaw wants to be an artist, a poet, a political reformer; Bulstrode wants to be a man of God. None of them fully achieves what they want. The question the novel asks is: what does this failure mean? Is it a tragedy? A moral failure? An inevitable consequence of the gap between human aspiration and human limitation? Or is it something more complex — a kind of education, a process by which the self is refined and deepened through the experience of failure?
